XVe learn that llis Excellency the Governor General, after attending Divine Service at St: Paul's on Sunday last, visited the Sunday School attached to that Church, accompanied by the Hector, several Officers and other gentlemen of respectability. When. His Excellency made his appearance, the child) err, numbering between three and four hundred, after rising and saluting him sung a spirited and loyal hymn to a Javo> ite national air. His Excellency then inspected the Library and passed among the diferent classes, apparently much interested, and was pleased to express himself highly gratified with the Order and arrangements of the institution. Upon His Excellency's retiring, the children again rose, and sli uc/i up another lively anthem. Tins visit was most encouraging to all connected with this school, and Ike animation of it will not soon be. forgotten. We close, by responding to the good wishes end wonls of the distinguished visiter, that, " This School House, went up in a very short time, but we hope it will continue a very long time." Peace prevails throughout British India, although the preparations for war weie busy throughout the north western distrirts. An army of about 15.000 men was assembling on the banks of t tie Sutledge. and anothei was Collecting at Agra ; the former to compel t Ire Sickhs to adopt some regular fixed s\sfem of government, and the la ter to force the government of Gwalior to make proper arrangements. Much attention has been directed towards the Ponjaub. The chiefs are represented as disunited, the soldiers are mutinous, and the provinces are distracted bv their I'enrs, for they dread an invasion from the Aflghans at Peshawur, and of the British at Lahore. A crisis was expected in Lahore, when the Governor General shall have tertehed the banks of the Sutledge. Several corps of the British troops were in movement in that direction. The number of troops at Ferozopore, Loodiana, and Umhalla, was estimated at 14,000 men. Major General George llntiter commanded at the two former places, while Major General Sir Kobeit Dick hail the command of the Sirhind and Meerut divisions. 'J be news from Cahnol current during the month was that Dost Mahorrnried had been mutdered; but, though believed by inany.it eventually turned out to be a fabrication." Important ReMEDY FOR CaNCERS. þÿ Col. Ussay, of the parish of De Soto, informs the editor of the Cado Gazette, that he has fully tested a remedy for this troublesome disease, recommended to him by a Spanish woman, a native of the country. The remedy is þÿthis; Take an egg and break it, then pour out the white, retaining the yolk in the shell, put in salt and mix w ith the yolk as long as it will receive it ; stir them together until the salve is formed, put a portion of this on a sticking plaster, and apply it to the cancer about twice a day. He has made the experiment in two instances in ins own family, with complete success.

The Island or Hong Kono. þÿ No doubt many of our readers have seen alarming statements in the newspapers as to the extreme insalubrity ol the island of Hong Kong, which was ceded to the British government by the late treaty with China ; and statements hove been made to the etldct that, as a British settlement and military station, the island would he abandoned. We are glad to leant, however, from a letter written by a very intelligent resident on the island to a mercantile house at Liverpool, under date of die 21st ol .September, that these statements are much exaggerated, and that the insalubrity is either confined to particular situations or the result of petsonal imprudences, which, in a tropical climate like that of the southern ex tremity of China, cannot he committed w ithout great danger. The following is an extract from the letter t þÿ - Although deaths have been very rile at Hong Hong of late, it is some consolation for the living to be able, in every instance, to trace the causes These are several, viz badly built and damp houses, imprudent exposure to the sun, and unhealthy sites. The live foreigners who have died lived iu a neighbour iiood about two miles and a halt from our place, and it is looked upon as full ol malaria. Besides this, bioken constitutions, damp houses, and imprudent exposure to the sun, had n siiare in some of these deaths. The deaths amongst the soldiery we take no account of, as they are indiHerently lodged . they expose themselves to the sun, and drink

freely of that poison, samshu, a spirit distilled from rue. It was the same at Chusuri, when the 26th (Cameronians) lost nearly all their men; and yet there are, at this þÿmoment Europiaus, þÿ soldiers and others, þÿ on the same site at Chusan, all perfectly healthy merely because experience has taught the authorities to use precautions. We have one ol the healthiest sites in Hong Kong. Our house is dry, lofty, and airy ; and we don't defy the sun, hut make a point to have a conveyance if we go to a distance in the daytime, either a boat, a sedan, or a carriage, and we are glad to say that we are free from sickness. The writer was ill for months before he left Macao. þÿRussia. Bektin, Jan. 20. þÿ We have here accounts from and concerning Russiasome of which are agreeable, others the reverse. M. Katakazi is said to have succeeded in completely justifying himself to his Government, and in proving that he acted strictly in the spirit of the instructions given him by Count Nesselrodo. It is added, tiiat lie has expressed a wish to be allowed to return as a private individual to Greece till all tiie existing dillerences are settled. The late discomfiture of the Russians in Cireassia is rather diminished than exaggerated by the German papers. Matters are now in such a state that very dilierent operations must be resorted to. It is well known that by the Emperor's orders the sanguinary and offensive war was changed into the defensive, but this became more difficult by the capture of important fortresses by the Circassian mountain tiibes, it is known here that these tribes receive from the English, by way ol Constantinople, money, ammunition, and instructions We have nothing but the melancholy accounts from Roland. The people are not allowed to have any arms, not even fowling pieces, without giving previous notice to the Russian authorities, who brand the arms. We bear statements that look like fables respecting the magnificence displayed at the Court ot St. Retersburgh on the marriage ot a Russian Rrineess with the presumptive heir to lite crown of Denmark, and also of Hesse, an event ot the highest importance to Germany. The Emperor presented bis

daughter with a suit of diamonds worth 500.- 000 silver rubles (75.000/), The Imperial family oi Russia is now allied hv marriage with Prussia, Wurtemberg, Nassau, Na\e- Weimar, Oldenburg, Hesse, Alien) org, Denmark, Holland, tile lainilv ol Napoleon, Ate. It is also reported that an Austrian prince is to marry a Russian princess; but we doubt this. 1 lie important consequences which this policy, so consistently followed, will have for Germany, is evident. þÿ Luening Mail.

The budget presented by the Minister of I' -nance to the French Chamber is of a character which may extend confidence and hope beyond the confines of the French territory. Three years of a profound tranquility hive brought with them increased wealth a flourishing commerce, and an income which already more than balances the expenditure of the nation. The surplus of the revenue for 1815 is calculated to be not much less titan 1,000,0001',, and the whole income of the Treasury for that year to exceed the income for 1841 by upwards of 28.000.000f. To elfoct this great improvement in the financial condition of his country, the French Minister has necessarily been compelled to

s t, o 3$ t> a at A ft" modify some, and to prune other branches of the dillbrent depui intents; but it does not appear that he has earned his economy beyond the bounds of prudence: lor, while lie has reduced the expenses ot the inteiior and the Marine, he lias made ampler provision than heretofoie for the departments ol Ruulie I rist ruction, of Public Works, and Religious Worship. So that die flourishing vendition of the revenue may fairly he asciihed to the prevalence of peace, and its usual iiuits, industry, commerce, and social older. We hope that the lesson thus strikingly inculcated will not be Inst upon the Ft tuck people, and least of a'l upon that party whose efforts have been principally directed to the prevention of those blessings with which France is now crowned. Let them ask, what is the condition of Fiance now as compared with its condition in 1 840 ; and what would it be now, if a war Ministry were to tegaiii the ascendancy ? Nor are these symptoms of reviving prospei ity matters of indifference to ourselves, while we regard them as guatantee.s that the tranquility of Europe will not be needlessly distuibed, we also look upon litem as cheering omens ut a better state of tilings in our own country. We too, aie beginning to extricate ourselves from the embarrassments of a languid tiade and an insufficient revemi"; we too, can congratulate ourselves on the excess <d the national income over the national expenditure; we have lately seen an advance þÿ a slight ad ance indeed, hut the

li- st lira I lias been made lor several yeais þÿ towards discharging the national deht; and we are now looking with sober satisfaction oil the improved state of our maikets and manufactures in the north. When we consider these tilings, we willingly allow ourselves to believe that the prosperity of the two countries cannot but be reciprocal; that if England flourish, France cannot be without commerce, and its substantial benefits; that if France be prosperous, the capital and industry of England cannot fail to be advantageously employed; and that t fie mutual knowledge of their respective interests may sudice to combine the two nations in a cordial endeavour to perpetuate the peace of Europe. þÿ (J lobe.

from Bell's Weekly Messenger, London January 22, 1844. Volcanic E ; option at the Sandwich Islands þÿ Extract from a letter from the Rev. T. Goan, dated Hilo (Sandwich Islands), -May 10, 1849: þÿ " God is not only working wonders in the moral and civil, hot also in the physical world around us. Yon have heard of the great volcanic eruption near our station in 1810. Another scene of a similar kind has recently taken place about the same distance from us. but in a different direction, and directly in the rear of our station. On the 10th of January of the present year, just at the dawn of day, we discovered a rapid disgorgement ol liquid lire fr-an near the summit of Manna Lin, at an elevation of 14. 000 feet above tiro sea. This eruption increased from dav to dav for several weeks, pouring out vasi floods of fi ry lava, which spread down the side of the mountain, and flowed oil in broad and buttling rivers, throwing a terrific glare upon the heavens, and filling those lofty mountainous regions with a sheet of light. This spectacle continued from week to week without any abatement, till the molien ll »al had progressed 20 or 90 miles down the side of the mountain, and acioss a high plain which stretches between the bases of Manna I.oa and Manna Kea. It was not till alter many weeks that 1 was able to visit this scene of terror and of sublimity. At length, in company wuh Mr. Raris, the missionary lor Kan þÿ a station south of Hid þÿ I made the attempt. We penetrated through a deep forest, stretching between Hilo and the mountain, arid reached the molten stream as it

flowed over those vast and high regions !\ ing at the base of the mountain. Here we were able to approach the fiery stream and dip up and cool us burning fluid, as we would approach the banks of a river and take of its waters. From this we followed the stream to the top of the mountain, arid found us source in a vast cratet, amidst the eternal snows oi those wild and desolate regions. Down the sides of the mountain the lava had now ceased to flow upon the surtaoe ; hut it had formed tor itself a subterranean duet, at the depth of 50 or 100 lend. This duet was encased wiili viti ifaction, as smooth as glass, and down this fearful channel a river of fire was rushing at the rate of 15 or 20 miles an hour, from the summit to the foot of the mountain. This subterranean stream we saw distinctly through several large apcitures ill the side of the mountain, while the burning flood rushed fearfully beneath our feet. Our standing above it was like standing upon ire on a t iver, while the liquid flood flows under \ our feet. Our visit was attended with peril & ir ort- ceivable fatigue, but we never regretted having made it, and we returned deeply aflected wi;h the majesty, (lie sublimity, the power, and the love of that God who looketh on the eaith and it trembled), who touches the lulls, ami thev smoke; whose presence melts the hills and whose look causes die mountains to flow down.'" þÿ American Taper.

" My Lords and Gentlemen, " It affords me great satisfaction again to meet you in parliament, and to have the opportunity of profiting by your assistance and advice. Foreign Intelligence. þÿ Spain þÿ It appears that what vve anticipated in this unfortunate country has occurred. Another revolution has broken out, and the present administration. if not the Queen's government, is about to he overthrown, and the radical juntas re established in all the great cities of the Kingdom At eleven ojelock at night, on the last day of January, M. Bravo summoned a hasty council, in which he infoi tried his colleagues, the other ministeis, that st me intercepted letters, which had been obtained at the Post oliice, and which were now before them, developed a conspiracy against the government, upon which it was necessary to take instant and decisive measures '1 he criminals were persons of influence and condition in the capital iiselt, and it was necessa rv to order their immediate arrest. Warrants were accordingly issued on the spot against sixty persons, either the writers of these letters, or implicated by their contents. Six deputies ot the Chambers were shortly afterwards arrested and lodged in the city gaol. Upon the breaking up of the council, the eulire garrison was placed under arms, the military posts were everywhere doubled, and during the night a living column of troops left the capital, vv.th orders to proceed to Valencia by forced marches. It futther appears, that an insurrectionary junta had been formed at Alieant, and in its proclamation the revolters in their demonstrations raised the cry of " Down with tyranny I" " Down with the executioners !" ' Down with the

government !" " Liberty and the Constitutional Queen for ever!" At the departure ot the mail it was reported in Madrid that the insurrection had extended to Valencia, and that a similar movement had occurred at Sanlander.

A large detachment of troops has been ordered to march upon Alicant. The commandant of the Alicant detachment has received orders to decimate and shoot upon the spot the National Guard at Alicant, unless they surrender upon summons. A courtmartial is to sit at Madrid, and the whole city is proclaimed to he under martial law. All accused or suspected persons are to be taken before this court, and after -entence on them, to be shot on the spot. The same martial law is extended to the provinces of Alicarit, Mercia, Albaee, Valencia, and Almeira. In a word, nearly the whole kingdom is proclaimed to be in a state of revolution, and the ordinary course ol law is superseded by
str,
court maitials to be instiiuted in all the provinces. From ihe appearance of affairs, either M. Bravo must instantly resign, or a civil war will pervade the whole kingdom.

Thorwaldsen is the only one of the great sculptors who is quite exempt from the gross errors into which Canova and even Michael Angelo himself has fallen, in too nearly imitating antique sculpture. The triumph of Alexander, the night and day, the procession of the loves, are instances. He has given modern impressions to the antique, without loosing its original meaning. No sculptor has shown how to manage modern realities or idealities so much in the antique spirit without being merely antique, as I'borwaldsen. He is considered the modern Phidias, and on his late travels in Germany was received with a jubilee that a king only could expect, and at Munich he arranged a new and more mvthologically the chamber of Niobe and her group.
from <t British .townal. Tlionvaldscn's Statue of Mercury. In conclusion, we cannot resist the gratification oi presenting to our readers the following anecdote of the famous Thorwald-

'jt Atn sen, whose return to his native country lias been recently hailed with so unanimous a tribute of admiration and applause. " Here, to make my peace with anecdotemoitgers, let me tell one relating to the origin of the finest statue of the greatest sculptor who has arisen since the genius of Greece dropped and wasted a way, beneudt the yoke of Rome. An illustrious friend of mine, calling on Thorwaldseti some veats ago, found him, as he said to me, in a glow, almost in a trance, of creative power. On his inquiitng what had happened, my friend, my dear ftiend,' said the sculptor, ' 1 have att idea, 1 have a work in my head, which will be worthy to live, 1 was waiking out yesterday when 1 saw a boy sitting on a stone in an attitude which struck me very much. \\ hat a beautiful statue that would make, 1 said to myself. But what would it do for? It would do, it would do, it would do exactly for Mercury., di awing his sword, just after fie has played Argus to sleep 1 came home immediately. 1 began modelling lwotkcd all the evening till at my usual hour 1 went to bed. But my idea would not let me rest. 1 was forced to get up again, I struck a light, and worked at niv model f t iluee or four hours ; alter which 1 again went to bed. but again I couid not test: again 1 was forced to get up, and have been working ever since. O, my friend, if 1 can but execute my idea it wiil be a glorious statue! And a noble statue it is, although Thorwaldseu himself did not think that tlte execution came up to the idea.

For 1 have heard of a remarkable speech of his, made some years alter to another friend, who found him one day somewhat out of spirits. Being asked whether any thing had occurred to distress him, he answered, ' rMy genius is decaying.' ' VV ir.it do you mean?' said the visitor. Why! here is my statue of Christ ; it is tire first of my works that I have ever felt satisfied with. Till now, my idea has always been !ar beyond what 1 couid execute. But it is no longer so: 1 should never have a great idea again. 1 horwaldsen's Mercury, it appears was suggested by a boy whom he had seen sitting on a stone- But does that detract from the sculpture's genius? Gvery other living man mignl have seen the boy, and no statue of Mercury would have sprung out of the vision, tso that, though Genius does not wholly create its works out of nothing, its ' mighty world' is not merely what it perceives, but what, as Wordsworth expresses it, in his lines, on the Wye, ' it half creates.' From Buenos Ayres. þÿ The arrival of the ship Roger Sliermon. brings intelligence from Buenos Ayres to January 2Sth, and from Montevideo to the 17th The state of affairs at the first named city, is said to be dreadful. Under the iron rule of Rosas, there exists no security for life or property, and men are frequently dragged from their families and shot in the public streets The war proceeds with its wonted violence and brutality. A skirmish took place outside the walls of Montevideo on the 15th, in which the sortie were deleated and driven back with a loss ot 28 killed and 50 wounded. Great complaints are made by the Buenos Ayres papers of the strong partiality evinced by the British Commodore, i'urvis, to the Montevideans. They also attribute the continuance of the war to the conduct of other English functionaries and the arming of foreigners. The French residents of Montevideo, still continue in the army, notwithstanding the interference of the French authorities.
